source.title: More Than a Toy: Random Matrix Models Predict How Real-World Neural Representations Generalize
source.authors: Alexander Wei; Wei Hu; Jacob Steinhardt

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text and appendices are present.
record.tranche_reason: Applies power-law scaling analysis to image neural representations and kernel regression, rather than language-model pretraining loss or parameter/token/compute sweeps.
record.gate_note: The study reports scaling exponents for optimally regularized ridge-regression generalization risk on vision data. It does not measure language-model pretraining loss, model-size/token/compute scaling, or compute-optimal parameter/token allocation. The reported ImageNet-pretrained versus random-initialization comparison is not a null control.
record.test_reason: The study does not test any version. Its scaling results concern optimally regularized kernel ridge regression on fixed eNTK features of ResNets, with risk scaled against sample size N only. This is a linear model on frozen representations, not neural-network training loss. The power-law form is assumed: exponents are log-log slope fits with no fit-quality test. No parameter, token or compute sweep is run. The study's focus is the GCV risk estimator and explaining kernel-regression scaling rates via eigendecay and alignment. These are related-construct findings, so they go under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The main conclusion, which the record omits, is that the GCV estimator accurately predicts the generalization risk of ridge regression on real neural representations, while norm- and spectrum-based approaches fail. The authors also prove GCV converges under a local Marchenko-Pastur law. They then argue that pretraining helps through better alignment despite slower eigendecay, and that eigendecay and alignment rates suffice to predict kernel-regression scaling rates.
record.recipe_differences: Uses eNTK representations and kernel ridge regression on vision datasets, studying risk scaling with sample size; it does not reproduce language-model loss sweeps over parameters, tokens, or compute.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported rates vary across datasets and between random initialization and pretrained representations. The Food-101 component-based estimate differs substantially from its reported actual rate.

fits_no_version.finding: For optimally tuned kernel ridge regression on ResNet eNTK features, risk falls with N at fitted log-log rates. Magnitudes run from about 0.014 (CIFAR-100, random init) to 0.19. Pretrained features give higher rates than random-init features (e.g. CIFAR-10: 0.162 vs 0.059).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Data-scaling rates of kernel regression on neural representations depend on the representation (pretrained vs random) and on the dataset.

fits_no_version.finding: The kernel-regression scaling rate is approximated by α̂=γ̂+δ̂, from estimated eigendecay and alignment rates. Pretraining gives slower eigendecay but much better alignment.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Eigendecay and alignment exponents predict kernel-regression data-scaling rates on natural image representations.

record.problems: The empirical scaling results are for image eNTK kernel regression rather than language-model pretraining loss or model/token/compute scaling. Flowers-102 is excluded from the scaling experiment because it has 2040 images. Table 3 reports a large gap between the component-based estimated rate and actual rate for Food-101, despite the authors' general statement that estimates approximate actual rates.
record.rows_left_out: No claim-relevant Table 2 rows were added; its correlation comparisons concern prediction of generalization risk by GCV and alternative estimators, rather than the claim's power-law scaling form. Other reported eigendecay and alignment quantities were not entered as rows because none of the claim versions names those measures.

untested.parts: Neural LM loss vs parameters, tokens or compute: not studied.
Extrapolation from small to large runs: not studied.
Shape effects at fixed parameter count: not studied.
Only kernel ridge regression on frozen image eNTK features vs sample size. The power-law form is assumed, not tested, and no trained neural model's loss is scaled.
Downstream predictability from scale or loss: not studied.
Exponents differ across datasets and initialisations, but only in kernel regression. Fitting choices for neural scaling laws and bending away from a power law are not examined.

missing.what: Table 2 ground-truth scaling exponents and the GCV, spectrum-only and norm-based predicted exponents. These are needed to check the Food-101 value in Table 3. The extracted Table 2 headers appear shifted: r=1.000 is ground truth against itself.

record.verdict_notes: Record relation 'tests' at T3 and its V5/V7 supports are overturned. The system is linear kernel regression on frozen features, scaled only in sample size, and the power-law form is fitted rather than tested. The Food-101 'gap' (α=0.985 vs α̂=0.087) is most likely a typo in Table 3, since Table 2 gives about 0.099. The authors themselves call the estimates accurate for all datasets. The paper is peer reviewed (ICML 2022) and code is released.

versions.untested_parts: Language-model held-out pretraining loss versus parameter count, tokens, or compute.
Whether small language-model runs predict much larger runs.
Compute-optimal parameter and token allocation, and its trend with compute.
Effects of depth, width, and architecture at fixed parameter count on language-model loss.

Tests power-law scaling of optimally regularized kernel-regression generalization risk in image settings, not language-model pretraining loss; does not test video, repeated data, fine-tuning, or transfer scaling as specified.
Predictability of language-model downstream task performance from scale or pretraining loss.

Tests variation in scaling rates across vision datasets and representation initialization/pretraining; does not test language-model fitting choices, parameter-counting choices, compute-optimal allocation, disagreement between the cited LM laws, or curve bending away from a power law.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Tested image datasets and eNTK ridge-regression settings
reader_labels.reason: The study reports positive power-law exponents for optimally regularized generalization risk across the listed image settings (rows T3-FMNIST-init-alpha through T3-Food101-pretr-alpha). This is evidence for a power-law form in this tested image-regression setting, not for language-model pretraining loss.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Vision ridge-regression configurations varying dataset and initialization/pretraining
reader_labels.reason: Reported optimal-risk rates and component-based rate estimates differ across datasets and between random and pretrained representations, showing configuration-dependent rates in this setting (rows T3-FMNIST-init-alpha through T3-Food101-pretr-alphahat).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: The component-rate estimate α̂ = 0.087 is far from the reported actual rate α = 0.985, limiting the claim that these estimated components predict the scaling rate in this condition (rows T3-Food101-pretr-alphahat and T3-Food101-pretr-alpha).
